Messages.Author: Orpheus
Messages.Body:
Very post-modern night indeed !! ;-)

My version of what happened in the finals :

Andrea's B52 deck was the biggest obvious threat at the table. His prey
wanted, understandably, to chance places. Stefan didn't want Andrea as
predator before he was established, so he influenced the whole table (mainly
Sébastien) towards not voting for it "yet". The discussion took about 15
minutes for nothing. Anyway the next time the vote was called the Giovanni
had a Delaying...

Now for the deal :

The B52 killed his first prey. Then he stops at Stefan's "wall", which
includes 3 minions at the time, while Andrea has 8, then 11. Andrea's hand
is then almost all-red, including Dodges and, I think, Fake Outs. No Master,
I think no Computer Hack at the time.

Andrea thinks he has no chance. The judge agrees. A few turns later Andrea
has 13 minions, as opposed to Stefan's 4, which proves that he had a chance
to win, if only in waiting.

Arguments against : "yes but if Stefan hadn't destroyed Arika, Sébastien
would have killed Andrea".

Wrong. The voter had no votes, and could only bleed for 3, and then 4 when
he got Maris Streck out. Andrea had a deflection in hand for quite a long
time, later got a Tribute to the Master, never was quite low on pool... He
had all the time he needed.

The Giovanni didn't play at all. I saw one of Le Din Tho's actions to
discard from Sébastien : he saw, among other : 2 Deflections, 1 Archon
Investigation, and no Wake. He had two other ready minions (one with +1
bleed). What would YOU have done ? Well, he discarded a Deflect, instead of
the Archon and 2 massive bleeds !! All because of the fear of his Tzimisce
predator ?! Come on, you play GIOVANNI !! How many Eagle Sight do you think
a guy with 3 minions, among whom only 2 with AUS, can play in a turn ? What
are Seduction and Call of the Hungry Dead for when your prey is tapped with
no Wake ? And even if you were really unlucky and your prey got back a Wake
/ Second Trad or an Archon, isn't it worth trying ?

Andrea, with all his combat in hand, could be "afraid" of only two things :

- Carrion Crows ; Stefan didn't play any, there wasn't any in his discard,
and Sébastien had already played against him
- Manoeuver / aggropock / Rötshit.

Come on, how many weenies would have gone into torpor ? How many Röts can
you play in a turn ? What does it matter if you "lose one or two weenies a
turn when it means bleeding for 6-8 without modifier each turn and getting
new minions for 1 pool (two including the "pay one to see one) every two
turns at worse ?

The truth is : Stefan is a brain-eating zombie. He was the only one thinking
straight at the table, maybe with the exception of his first and late
predator (who unfortunately didn't speak english well enough to convince
anyone).

To really be able to do at least once what people thought he could do,
Stefan should have had :

- At least 1 Eagle's Sight ; probably 2
- 1 Röt
- 2 maneuver / Agg
- Wakes, preferably lots of
- Intercept for blocking votes or +1 stealth Giovanni bleeds

When I looked Stefan had about 5 blue cards. Not a lot left to hurt anyone
anymore.

How many cards can anyone have in hand ? What kind of player could resist
all the table against him ?

Not Andrea. Not Stefan. Maybe not even both together.

So in my witnessing eyes : Andrea could have talken some risks and would
probably have killed his prey (at least chances were he could, so he should
have been obligated to) before Arika could do any damage ; The Giovanni
could have put a lot of pressure on HIS prey and probably killed her ;
Stefan had no means at that point of making any VP except by dealing things
no one should ever have accepted ; seeing the seating, his state of
sleepiness and the way he came out library-wise, Séb had no chance at all.

But Stefan was very good in talking and won.

The deal should never have been validated. The judge didn't even look at the
cemetaries or libraries of the players. Sure, he didn't have to make any
indications, but he should have said : "there is a chance, however slight,
that you kill your prey by yourself, and then you could be able to make more
VPs. So : optimize !!".

One other thing : I think translations shouldn't happen at such a table :
not by other present players, not by judges, not by willing witnesses like
me. I may like it or not but english being the official language, speaking
it fluently, at least in game terms, is a part of knowing how to play the
game internationally, so the only translations should be explanations on the
working of cards, rules, erratas. Nothing else. But I may be wrong on that
account.

One thing I'm sure of : the "normal" results should have read : Table
between Andrea and the Giovanni. Handshakes for the rest.

Now it's also what I like about this game : what you have in hand and on the
table is only a small fraction of what you can do.

Congratulations again to Stefan.

Messages.Author: David Cherryholmes
Messages.Body:
I don't think there *is* a fix for this problem in terms of changing
rules. But it is a problem. IME, *most* finals are dealt to
resolution, rather than being resolved by the play of cards. My
personal choice is to avoid any lengthy trips to attend tournaments
anymore for just this reason. It strikes me as largely a waste of time,
although that's only a logical consequence of disliking such resolution;
if you have no problem with Jyhad being much closer to Diplomacy than
Magic, then for you there is no problem.

But there is a solution. It involves the judges, using judgment. As a
judge, the last thing I want to do is step in and start playing
someone's game for them. The absolute last thing. However, nearly
*every* game will come down to a situation where a player is about to be
ousted by their predator, giving him the opportunity to eke out one last
VP by becoming that predator's whore. IMO, this is a perversion of the
basic predator-prey structure of the game. No, that relationship is not
pristine in any case, but the scenario whereby the dominant player just
sits back and unleashes his tool upon the table will suck the fun out of
a game so fast that I think this particular scenario should be avoided
as much as possible. As a judge, it is a fairly straightforward process
to decide if either of the two parties involved have a *reasonable*
chance at more VP's. As a judge, if one or more of the players at the
table has chosen to put you in that position, then I think a lot of the
guilt stemming from slapping them down is mitigated.

Just my two cents.... this is a complicated, subtle, and subjective topic.

--

David Cherryholmes

One thing I feel would be helpful: get more damn OFFENSE back into
the game. If people feel otherwise, I'd like to hear about it. But
my observation about the game is that it's almost impossible to bring
a quick-hitting deck to a good tournament and do well with it
anymore. There's too many ways to effectively stave off defeat,
if not to avoid being ousted in the end, at least to slow the
aggressor down enough to bring the table down on his/her head.

It often seems like a lot of the game nowadays is defense first and
ousting power second. Good players hope to survive and hold on long
enough to align the table against their prey and predator or to see
an opening caused by someone else's bad play. I'm not saying I
want to switch it completely around so that offense dominates. But
I'd like to see more balance such that a fast deck can have some
hope of getting the occasional sweep, even against really skilled
players.

Of course, the obvious way to do that is to enhance stealth-bleed
decks. That would probably be bad. So I'm not sure exactly what
I'm asking for here, I'll admit. Just some food for thought, I
guess.

Fred

I agree, but that's not really playing to maximize your VP. I have a
followup to that, but it rests solely on a bunch of players making the
"right" choice when there's no real consequence if they take the low
road. My answer is this: you could also "maximize" your VP's by
cheating. So, why don't you? Yeah, there's a rule against it, but I
think even if there weren't, most players would realize that there's
nothing riding on this game but the fun we have playing it. It isn't
Magic, or Lord of the Rings, or Star Wars, or Yugio, or any of the other
plethora of games where cash prizes can be awarded. Cheating is
pointless, even if it would be trivial to get away with it. When was
the last time someone counted your deck to ensure it was 90 cards?
Crypt backs not tellingly mixed? We don't bother, in the main, because
everyone understands that we've made the trip to come together to
compete in good faith, have a good time, and proclaim one player the
best of the day. When you turn the table into an omelette and sign up
with Team Whore, sure... you've maximized some VP's. But at what cost?
Everyone getting on the same page with their answers to this question is
the only real answer I see to the scenario of "get one and roll",
without radically altering the play to win rule (which I'm generally
against, but would consider as a solution of last resort).

> -accept the offer and immediatly backstab the predator for trying to
> manipulate him like a puppet. it's the jyhad, man =)

This would also be a good solution, but I just heard an unrelated story
today on IRC about how people in this person's playgroup would scoop if
someone breaks a deal. The metagaming for maximum advantage with "mah
wurd is mah bond" is, I think, technically correct; you will gain more
VP's in the long run by keeping deals than by breaking them, unless once
again the majority of players get on the same page about what is an
acceptible sacrifice to maintain the "fun" of the game. I know I just
invoked "fun", and that this sets of bells in some player's heads. I'm
all for competitive play, bring your filthiest, worst decks the lopsided

Mmmm. Upon reflection, perhaps I'm missing the boat blaming the
lack of offense. That may not be it...exactly. Thinking about it,
it seems like what guys are doing can be abstracted down to:
"Try to survive as long as possible and - if feasible - also try
to fix any imbalances arising in the game that do not seem to be
in your favor. Wait until something happens that seems to be
collapsing the game in a way that IS to your benefit and jump on
it." Sometimes what winds up happening can be the result of
metagame issues. But a lot of other times, it's someone's
incompetance that throws the game out of whack and causes it to
start collapsing. At the point, the good players jump into gear
and start trying to stave it off, move it along, or find a way to
twist the results around (e.g. Dramatic Upheaval) to their favor
as it collapses (depending on their specific options at that
moment).

How does that work as a description of reality?

If it's reasonable, then this is all pretty entertaining as long
as there _are_ "incompetant" players or less competant players
or some kind of dynamic going that will eventually collapse the
table. When there's not, you get five players endlessly negotiating
to bring about SOME kind of result. But when everyone's fairly
competant and no one's in a bad metagame position or anything -
which in the finals of large, competitive tournaments seems pretty
common - then the continual rebalancing that goes on and on starts
becoming the rule. Players continually watch for threatening
patterns forming in the play and immediately move to adjust anything
they don't like. Since only one guy can actually win the game,
at least three and sometimes four and sometimes even all five
players are attempting at any given moment to stablize dynamics
they fear will ultimately collapse the table in a way not to their
liking. This makes for games that go nowhere over time - at least
until the last 10 minutes when finally, everyone realizes that if
nothing happens someone will win the tournament by default. Then
something may happen.

If all of this theorizing is correct, then the problem isn't
*exactly* lack of offense in the game. Say that the problem is
more along the lines of the game being too easy for players to
rebalance and that there aren't enough aspects of the game that can
cause involuntary collapse in a way third parties can't effect.

I'm still not sure what a solution (that's not worse than the
problem) would look like.

Fred

"Chris Arthur" <chr...@comcen.com.au> wrote in message

> > can cause involuntary collapse in a way third parties can't
> > effect.
> >

> Do you think it has something to do with the Game Win rule? I know
> I no longer build decks that can sweep partly because other players
> will jump all over you but also because you only really need game
> wins to make a final and not vps.

In a way, it might have to do with the game win rule - but not due
to that reason. For one thing, I specifically mentioned the finals
further down in my post, which you cut. The finals, as you know,
is played without reference to the game win rule nor has any need
for one. Of course, the particular set of objectives players have
in the finals is probably closer in nature to the game win rule than
to how preliminary games used to be played prior to the inception
of it. But this has always been true, so it doesn't matter. (For
that matter, the issue about endless-negotiation-no-action may also
predate the game win rule.)

To the extent "endless-negotiating-no-action" experiences may be
more prevalent now than before the game win rule, it would probably
be because there were more arguably "acceptable" outcomes to which
players could negotiate once it became clear that the sheer metagame
and player incompetancies wasn't going to collapse the game by
itself. That is, it was fairly reasonable in the past to negotiate
a two-two, two-two-one, or three-two split without either of the
leading players being that dissatisfied with the outcome prior to
the game win rule. Now the former two are usually pointless to both
players and the latter pointless to the second place player. So
it's a lot harder to do anything but continue to survive and hang
on when the situation comes up.

However, given the nature of negotiated splits - which are far less
appealing results than games which have been actively disputed from
start to finish - I hardly think it's worth seeking a solution by
getting rid of the game win rule. The game win rule was instituted
for a very important reason. It's not perfect but all things
considered, it's solved the problem it was created to solve
incredibly well. Negotiated splits are _far_ less common now and
with them, a lot of suspicions and accusations of out-of-game
conspiracies, cliquishness, and other speculative but scary forms
of behavior. It's not often such a change works every bit as well
as planned. I would hope the rule is here to stay.

Fred

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
"Charles Lechasseur" <da...@novideospamtron.ca> wrote in message
news:danov-29090...@192.168.1.4...

> I think one possible solution would be to change the rule that
> says that you must get a GW if possible. The problem with this
> rule is that even when a player can possibly get a sweep, that
> player is still free to split the table and offer 1 or 2 VPs to
> someone else. The rules should force a player to always go for
> the maximum number of VPs possible. After all, I do think that
> getting extra VPs after a GW can change a lot of things (you
> might need those extra VPs to get into the finals, say).

First of all, this is not the problem I started out worrying
about - which was about players, particularly in the finals, playing
merely to survive and wait for things to fall their way causing
games to turn into endless negotiating marathons in which nothing
ever happens. The above rule hardly addresses that. The problem,
in my estimation, isn't that the negotiation is caused by giving
players incentive to play for second place or (in the prelims) an
extra VP or two. The problem is that players as a group are so
successful at continually rebalancing and stalling the game when
it doesn't seem to be progressing the way the want.

I don't really have an issue with players not having to win the
maximum number of VPs if possible. It does cause some slight
concerns about table splits but these don't seem to happen often
nowadays nor do they affect games nearly as profoundly as they used
to before the game win rule. Such judgements are extremely
subjective (as all the debute over it proves) and thus hard to
enforce. The game win rule fixed a lot of problems because it's
not subjective at all: it just gives players concrete motivation to
do the right thing. Ultimately, I don't see how tinkering with
subjective judgements about players' motivations is likely to yield
much satisfaction. At least, not in this case.

Fred

Put it this way: if you want to question whether it's worthwhile
to aspire to second place over fifth place - especially when it's
clear that you won't be finishing in first place - then that may
well be a reasonable philosphoical question. But if so, POSE IT
THAT WAY! Don't just "out of the blue" challenge people to explain
to you why anyone would bother playing for second over fifth place.
The answer to that is fairly obvious. Stefan is right: the question
as posed was utterly stupid.

I think some of the philosphical arguments tend to get more personal
than they need to be because people get a bit arrogant about
assuming their own point of view is the only worthwhile one.
It's easy to do. (I'm certainly guilty of it often enough.) But
one should recognize at least after the mistake has been made and
get back to the gist of the dispute.

OBGISTOFTHEDISPUTE: My experience is that there's no resolution to
this. The value of second place over last place in a multiplayer
game has been disputed since the beginning of time. Some will
think it very worthwhile, others will not see a whit of difference.
For myself, I place first place on a much higher plane than any of
the others but if I can't first, I will definitely value second over
last.

Fred

The kind of thing I'm talking about occurred (in its extreme form)
at the NA Continental Final I think the two years before this one.
(This year's final sounds like it at least had _some_ play and an
actual oust or two during its course so was not so bad.) When all
five finalists are still around after nearly two hours of play in
a game which has been marked by almost constant talk and negotiation,
that's a sign that the game has gone _too much_ over to being
dominated by diplomacy and doesn't have enough play in it. No,
I don't consider myself "anti-deal-making". I think there's room
for it in the game and it can be a good thing to some extent.
(Albeit I'll confess it's not a part of the game I excel at.)
But in my observation, the importance of it seems to accentuate
considerably when high-quality players play. If the dealmaking
has an actual resolution that moves the game along, that's fine.
But what often seems to happen is that as the things start to
resolve, the players not gaining by the resolution will suddenly
start negotiating with each other and renegotiating their deals
with the ones currently winning and alliance will break and reform
causing the table to restablize again. For this to occur in endless
cycles is just plain boring - both to watch and to play. The game
is ultimately SUPPOSED to be about cards. Not negotiating.

The "last 10 minutes" thing wasn't intended to suggest that the
players weren't paying attention to who would win any tiebreakers
until then. It's that at that point, time will bring things to a
conclusion if nothing further is resolved - so this seems to affect
people's thinking about how to negotiate at this point.

Fred

Play _a_ game. Not tournament V:TES.

I can't believe that you are advocating lengthening the time taken to play a
game of V:TES. It already takes longer than the majority of other CCGs on
the market and is frequently cited as a reason why people don't play or
don't find it appealing to learn (source: www.boardgamegeek.com).

The number of players in a game has a massive effect on how the game plays.
Players, including myself, have been known to choose decks based on the
tables sizes at a tournament 3-4 player tables give an advange to combat
decks as there are fewer rush targets and the table is cowed into submission
more easily. Conversely combat decks have a much tougher time in 6+ player
tables. More targets, longer games and their deck size is the same. It's a
worse proposition.

Diplomacy and table talk are part of a multiplayer CCGs and i've not seen a
negotiated win at a UK tournament in over a year and very, very few since
the introduction of the game win rule.

Matt Green
